plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line graph of four straight lines tracing free energy against temperature for the four sign combinations of enthalpy and entropy change. The vertical axis is labeled Free energy and the horizontal axis Increasing temperature (K); the only numeral shown is 0 on the vertical axis. A gray dashed line at that zero splits the field into a pink upper half labeled Nonspontaneous, with delta G greater than 0 printed beside the axis, and a green lower half labeled Spontaneous, with delta G less than 0. All four lines start at the left edge. A red line begins high in the pink field and climbs to the upper right, labeled delta H greater than 0, delta S less than 0, while a green line begins in the green field and falls to the lower right, labeled delta H less than 0, delta S greater than 0. Two yellow lines lie between them and both cross the dashed zero line: one starts in the pink field and slopes downward, labeled delta H greater than 0, delta S greater than 0, the other starts in the green field and slopes upward, labeled delta H less than 0, delta S less than 0. Starting half and slope sign together encode the two arithmetic signs, so only the yellow pair changes shading as temperature rises, each at its own x-intercept. The plot motivates why a process whose enthalpy and entropy changes share a sign reverses spontaneity at the temperature where free energy is zero.

interactionPlan.concept: The temperature dependence of Gibbs free energy (ΔG = ΔH - TΔS) dictates that processes with matching signs for enthalpy and entropy will switch between spontaneous and nonspontaneous at a specific threshold temperature.

demo_steps.title: Absolute zero
demo_steps.narration: At T=0, the TΔS term is zero, so free energy (ΔG) equals enthalpy (ΔH). The y-intercepts alone determine if a reaction starts in the spontaneous (green) or nonspontaneous (pink) region.

demo_steps.title: Always nonspontaneous
demo_steps.narration: If a process absorbs heat (ΔH > 0) and decreases disorder (ΔS < 0), the slope is positive. ΔG goes further into the pink region as it heats up, so it is never spontaneous.

demo_steps.title: Always spontaneous
demo_steps.narration: Conversely, releasing heat (ΔH < 0) and increasing disorder (ΔS > 0) yields a negative slope. ΔG stays in the green region, so it is spontaneous at all temperatures.

demo_steps.title: Spontaneous at high temperatures
demo_steps.narration: When signs match, temperature controls spontaneity. An endothermic process with increasing entropy (ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0) starts nonspontaneous, but crosses into the green region at high temperatures.

demo_steps.title: Spontaneous at low temperatures
demo_steps.narration: An exothermic process with decreasing entropy (ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0) starts spontaneous, but the unfavorable entropy term pushes ΔG into the pink region as temperature rises.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: When enthalpy and entropy changes share the same sign, they compete to control ΔG, and temperature acts as the deciding factor that flips the reaction's spontaneity.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Divide the plot horizontally with a dashed '0' line: upper half filled with distinct light pink, lower half with light green. Plot four straight lines originating from two y-intercepts (one above 0, one below 0). The red line goes from +y-int steeply up. The green line goes from -y-int steeply down. The two yellow lines (make them slightly different shades if necessary, or just standard yellow with dark enough borders to be legible) cross the zero line: one from +y-int sloping down, one from -y-int sloping up. Ensure line labels stay near their respective lines. When toggled, dim or hide unselected lines to emphasize the active one. The temperature slider drives a vertical line spanning the height of the plot with dots appearing at the intersection of the cursor and visible lines.

authoredContext:
Such a plot is shown in the figure. A process whose enthalpy and entropy changes are of the same arithmetic sign will exhibit a temperature-dependent spontaneity as depicted by the two yellow lines in the plot. Each line crosses from one spontaneity domain (positive or negative ΔG) to the other at a temperature that is characteristic of the process in question. This temperature is represented by the x-intercept of the line, that is, the value of T for which ΔG is zero:

So, saying a process is spontaneous at “high” or “low” temperatures means the temperature is above or below, respectively, that temperature at which ΔG for the process is zero. As noted earlier, the condition of ΔG = 0 describes a system at equilibrium.

These plots show the variation in ΔG with temperature for the four possible combinations of arithmetic sign for ΔH and ΔS.

A graph is shown where the y-axis is labeled, “Free energy,” and the x-axis is labeled, “Increasing temperature (K).” The value of zero is written midway up the y-axis with the label, “delta G greater than 0,” written above this line and, “delta G less than 0,” written below it. The bottom half of the graph is labeled on the right as, “Spontaneous,” and the top half is labeled on the right as, “Nonspontaneous.” A green line labeled, “delta H less than 0, delta S greater than 0,” extends from a quarter of the way up the y-axis to the bottom right of the graph. A yellow line labeled, “delta H less than 0, delta S less than 0,” extends from a quarter of the way up the y-axis to the middle right of the graph. A second yellow line labeled, “delta H greater than 0, delta S greater than 0,” extends from three quarters of the way up the y-axis to the middle right of the graph. A red line labeled, “delta H greater than 0, delta S less than 0,” extends from three quarters of the way up the y-axis to the top right of the graph.
